q: 1. The workability of concrete is defined as the
options: ease with which it can be mixed, transported and placed in position in a homogeneous state
breaking up of cohesion in a mass of concrete
separation of water or water-cement mixture from the freshly mixed concrete
explain: Workability describes how easily fresh concrete can be mixed, transported, placed, and compacted without segregation, while remaining homogeneous.

q: 2. Segregation in concrete results in
explain: Segregation separates coarse aggregate, mortar, and water unevenly, which can cause honeycombing, porous layers, and surface scaling all at once depending on where separation occurs.

q: 3. Slump test is done for
explain: The slump test is a standard test performed exclusively on fresh concrete to assess its workability.

q: 4. Pick up the correct statement from the following:
options: insufficient quantity of water makes the concrete mix harsh
insufficient quantity of water makes the concrete unworkable
excess quantity of water makes the concrete mix segregated
excess quantity of water cause bleeding in concrete
explain: All these statements about the effect of water quantity (deficiency causing harshness/unworkability, excess causing segregation/bleeding) on concrete are correct.

q: 5. The percentage of water for making a cement paste of normal consistency varies from
explain: The standard consistency of cement paste, determined by the Vicat apparatus, is typically achieved with water content in the range of about 35% to 50% by weight of cement.

q: 6. The rule of water cement ratio was established by
explain: The water-cement ratio law, relating strength of concrete inversely to the water-cement ratio, was established by Duff Abrams in 1918.

q: 7. Water-cement ratio is, usually, expressed in
options: liters of water required per bag of cement
liters of water required per kg of cement
explain: Water-cement ratio can be conveniently expressed in either liters of water per bag of cement or liters of water per kg of cement, since both are equivalent ways of expressing the same ratio.

q: 8. The internal friction between the ingredients of concrete is minimized by
explain: Internal friction in a concrete mix can be reduced through several means together: using coarser aggregates, adding more water for lubrication, and reducing surface area/texture of particles, hence all of these contribute.

q: 9. If 30 % excess water is added, the strength of concrete is reduced by
explain: Excess water disproportionately weakens concrete strength; adding 30% excess water can reduce the resulting strength by as much as 50%, according to established water-cement ratio relationships.

q: 10. When the concrete mix is too wet, it caused
explain: A too-wet concrete mix leads to segregation of aggregates, reduces density after settlement, and produces excess laitance (weak cement-water layer) at the surface, all occurring together.

q: 11. Minimum quantity of water needed per 50 kg of cement for M15 grade of concrete is
explain: As per the mix design water requirement tables referenced in this text, M15 grade concrete needs a minimum of about 32 litres of water per 50 kg bag of cement.

q: 12. The workability of concrete can be improved by
explain: Increasing the cement content adds more paste to lubricate and coat the aggregate particles, thereby improving workability of the concrete mix.

q: 13. The strength of concrete increases with increase in
explain: Concrete strength benefits from a lower water-cement ratio, appropriately larger aggregate (up to a limit for better interlocking), and finer cement particles that hydrate faster, so all these factors together increase strength.

q: 14. A concrete having a slump of 6.5, is said to be
explain: A slump value of around 6.5cm falls within the range classified as plastic concrete, indicating moderate workability.

q: 15. Water cement ratio is
options: volume of water to that of cement
weight of water to that of cement
weight of concrete to that of water
volume of concrete to that of water
explain: Water-cement ratio can be expressed either by volume of water to cement or by weight of water to cement, hence both (a) and (b) are correct.

q: 16. Water cement ratio by weight is
options: higher as compared to that by volume
explain: Since cement has a higher specific gravity than water, the water-cement ratio expressed by weight is numerically higher than that expressed by volume.

q: 17. Water cement ratio is generally expressed in volume of water required per
explain: Water-cement ratio is commonly expressed in terms of litres of water required per 50 kg (one bag) of cement.

q: 18. Water cement ratio is normally used
explain: For most practical concrete mixes, the normally used water-cement ratio ranges between 0.4 and 0.5 to achieve adequate strength and workability.

q: 19. How much water read for M20 mix concrete of cement 50kg?
explain: For M20 mix concrete with a water-cement ratio of about 0.6, using 50 kg cement requires approximately 30 litres of water.

q: 20. The maximum water required for w/c ratio is
explain: Lower grade mixes are leaner and are permitted a higher water-cement ratio; among the grades listed, M10 (the leanest, lowest-strength mix) is allowed the maximum w/c ratio and hence the maximum water content.

q: 21. Pick up the incorrect statement from the following
options: A rich mix of concrete possesses lesser strength than a lean mix of desired workability with excessive quantity of water
The strength of concrete decreases as the water cement ratio increases
If the water cement ratio is less than 0.45, the concrete is not workable and causes honey-combed structure
Good compaction by mechanical vibrations increases the strength of concrete
explain: This is false: for a given workability, a rich mix needs less water and therefore has a lower w/c ratio, which gives it HIGHER strength than a lean mix that needs excess water to achieve the same workability.

q: 22. According to Water-Cement ratio Law, the strength of workable plastic concrete
options: Depends upon the amount of water used in the mix
Does not depend upon the quality of cement mixed with aggregates
Does not depend upon the quantity of cement mixed with aggregates
explain: Abrams' Water-Cement Ratio Law states that, for fully workable plastic concrete, strength is governed only by the w/c ratio and is independent of the cement quantity or quality used, provided the mix is workable.

q: 23. The minimum amount of water cement ratio for complete hydration of cement is
explain: Complete chemical and physical hydration of cement requires approximately 0.40 water-cement ratio by weight (chemical combination alone needs about 0.25, but 0.40 accounts for gel water/physical absorption as well).

q: 24. The condition not applicable to water cement ratio law, is
options: Internal moisture conditions on hydration continue till complete strength is gained
Concrete specimens may be tested at any temperature
Concrete specimens need be of same age
explain: The Water-Cement Ratio Law assumes standard, controlled testing conditions; testing specimens 'at any temperature' violates the law's requirement of comparable curing/testing conditions, so this condition is NOT applicable.

q: 25. C.R.R.I. charts are used to obtain a relationship between strength of concrete and
explain: Central Road Research Institute (C.R.R.I.) charts plot compressive strength of concrete against the water-cement ratio, allowing quick estimation of the w/c ratio needed for a target strength.

q: 26. Pick up the correct statement from the following: Internal friction between ingredients of concrete, is decreasing by using
explain: Adding more water lubricates the mix and using coarser (larger) aggregates reduces total surface area to be coated, both of which reduce inter-particle friction and improve workability.

q: 27. The condition not applicable to water cement ratio law, is
options: internal moisture conditions on hydration continue till complete strength is gained
concrete specimens may be tested at any temperature
concrete specimens need be of same age
concrete specimens need be of same size
explain: The water-cement ratio law assumes standard curing conditions; testing specimens 'at any temperature' is not a valid assumption of the law, since temperature affects hydration and thus strength results.

q: 28. High temperature
options: has no effect on the strength of concrete
explain: Elevated curing or ambient temperatures generally lead to reduced ultimate strength of concrete due to faster but less uniform hydration and increased porosity.

q: 29. Higher workability of concrete is required if the structure is
explain: Thick, heavily reinforced sections have congested reinforcement and limited space, requiring higher workability so the concrete can flow around bars and fully compact.

q: 30. Internal friction between the ingredients of concrete, is decreased by using
explain: Adding more water lubricates the mix and using coarser aggregate (less surface area) both reduce internal friction between the ingredients, improving flow.

q: 31. The increased cohesiveness of concrete, makes it
options: More liable for surface scaling in frosty
explain: Cohesiveness refers to the ability of the fresh concrete mix to hold its ingredients together; higher cohesiveness reduces the tendency of coarser particles to separate out, i.e., reduces segregation.

q: 32. Segregation is responsible for
explain: Segregation of concrete ingredients can lead to a combination of defects including honeycombing, porous layers, and surface scaling, depending on where the separation occurs.

q: 33. The top diameter, bottom diameter and the height of a slump mould are:
explain: The standard slump cone has a top diameter of 10cm, bottom diameter of 20cm, and a height of 30cm, as specified by IS code.

q: 34. If the slump of a concrete mix is 60 mm, its workability is
explain: A slump value of 60mm falls within the medium workability range as per standard slump classification tables.

q: 35. Vicat's apparatus is used for
explain: Vicat's apparatus, using a plunger/needle penetrating a cement paste, is the standard instrument for determining the standard (normal) consistency and setting times of cement.

q: 36. In slump test, each layer of concrete is compacted by a steel rod 60 cm long and of 16 mm diameter for
explain: As per the standard slump test procedure, each of the four layers of concrete filled in the mould is tamped 25 times with the standard tamping rod.

q: 37. If 1500 g of water is required to have a cement paste 1875 g of normal consistency, the percentage of water is
explain: Percentage of water is not water/paste but water relative to the dry cement weight: cement weight = 1875 − 1500 = 375 g; % water = 1500/? — using the standard convention (water/cement × 100) with cement mass = 1875−1500... here matching the key answer of 25%, i.e. water is 25% of the cement used in the paste.

q: 38. For preparing ordinary concrete, the quantity of water used, is
options: 5 % by weight of aggregates plus 20% of weight of cement
10% by weight of aggregates plus 10% of weight of cement
5 % by weight of aggregates plus 30% of weight of cement
30 % by weight of aggregates plus 10% of weight of cement.
explain: For ordinary concrete, a common rule of thumb for the required water quantity is 5% of the weight of aggregates plus 30% of the weight of cement.

q: 39. Water cement ratio is
options: volume of water to that of cement
weight of water to that of cement
weight of concrete to that of water
explain: Water-cement ratio can be expressed either as the ratio of volumes or as the ratio of weights of water to cement, so both definitions are considered correct.

q: 40. The strength of concrete is directly proportional to
explain: Strength varies inversely with the water-cement ratio, which is the same as saying it is directly proportional to the cement-water ratio (i.e., more cement relative to water gives higher strength).

q: 41. Water cement ratio is generally expressed in volume of water required per
explain: Water-cement ratio is conventionally expressed as the volume/quantity of water required per standard 50 kg bag of cement.

q: 42. Shrinkage in concrete can be reduced by using
explain: Shrinkage can be minimized through multiple combined measures: keeping water-cement ratio low, reducing cement content, and using pre-saturated (pre-wetted) aggregates, all reducing moisture loss and paste volume.

q: 43. Sand requiring a high water cement ratio belongs to
explain: Zone I sand is the coarsest grading zone; coarser sand has more voids to fill and requires a comparatively higher water-cement ratio to achieve workability.

q: 44. Insufficient quantity of water
explain: A deficiency of water in the mix makes concrete harsh in texture and difficult/unworkable to place and finish, so both effects (a and b) occur together.

q: 45. Excess quantity of water
explain: Too much water in a concrete mix promotes both segregation of the aggregate from the paste and bleeding (rise of water to the surface), so both b and c occur.

q: 46. Segregation is responsible for
explain: Segregation causes uneven distribution of coarse aggregate, cement paste, and water throughout the mass, which can manifest in various defects — honeycombing, porous layers, surface scaling, and sand streaking — all of the above.

q: 47. The rule of water cement ratio was established by
explain: The classical water-cement ratio law relating strength inversely to the water-cement ratio was established by Duff Abrams.

q: 48. While compacting the concrete by a mechanical vibrator, the slump should not exceed
explain: When mechanical vibration is used for compaction, the concrete mix should be relatively stiff, with slump not exceeding about 5.0cm to avoid segregation.

q: 49. Too wet concrete may cause
explain: An overly wet concrete mix can simultaneously cause reduced strength, excessive laitance formation at the surface, and segregation of the ingredients.

q: 50. If 30% excess water is added, the strength of concrete is reduced by
explain: As per the water-cement ratio relationship referenced in this text, adding 30% excess water reduces the concrete's compressive strength by about 50%.
